article.headline: UK Prime Minister Condemns Lenient Sentences for Teenage Rapists
article.summary: Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer has expressed his outrage over the lenient sentences given to three teenage boys who raped two teenage girls in separate incidents in Hampshire. The boys were spared custodial sentences and instead received Youth Rehabilitation Orders, which the victims and their families have criticized as inadequate. The attorney general is reviewing the sentences, and the prime minister has described the case as "appalling".
article.body:
The case involves two girls, aged 15 and 14, who were raped by two 14-year-old boys in November 2024 and January 2025. A third boy, aged 13 at the time, was also convicted for his involvement in the second attack. The boys filmed the rapes on their phones and shared some of the footage online. At the sentencing hearing, Judge Nicholas Rowland said he wanted to "avoid criminalising these children unnecessarily" and instead gave them Youth Rehabilitation Orders, which can include unpaid work, curfews, or treatment.

One of the victims, now 16, has spoken out about the sentence, saying it was like a "rock straight in my face" and made her feel like the law did not take the crime seriously. She and her family are calling for the sentences to be changed and the boys to be sent to jail. The prime minister has described the girl's testimony as "harrowing and brave" and said that the girls at the heart of the case have shown "extraordinary bravery and strength in heinous circumstances".

The attorney general has 28 days to review the sentences and decide whether to refer them to the Court of Appeal. Cabinet Minister Darren Jones has said that he expects the decision to be made quickly, and that the girls "deserve justice, as do their families, both for them but also for other girls that are put in that position". Other politicians, including Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch and Liberal Democrat MP Ben Maguire, have also spoken out about the case, describing it as "sickening" and "utterly horrific".

The case has sparked widespread outrage and concern about the handling of sexual assault cases in the UK. Dame Rachel de Souza, the Children's Commissioner for England, has said that she is "deeply concerned" and that her office will reach out to the families to offer support. A government spokesperson has said that the law officers are reviewing the case "with the utmost care and attention".

The sentences given to the boys have been criticized as too lenient, with many arguing that they do not reflect the seriousness of the crimes. The boys would not have been sent to prison even if they had been given custodial sentences, as they would have served their time in secure centers for children. However, the victims and their families argue that the sentences do not provide adequate justice or accountability for the crimes committed.
article.takeaway: The UK Prime Minister has condemned the lenient sentences given to three teenage boys who raped two teenage girls, describing the case as "appalling" and calling for a review of the sentences.
